beats.text: Think of an apple. Its red, its weight, its sweetness — every quality is something sensed.
Berkeley pushed this hard. Take away everything that could be perceived, he said. What's left?
Nothing. For him there's no lump of 'matter' hiding behind the sensations. The sensations are the thing.
His famous line: to be is to be perceived. A thing exists in being seen, heard, or felt.
So does the tree vanish when you leave the forest? Here most people expect a trick answer.
No, said Berkeley. It stays — because it is never truly unperceived. God perceives it always.
You may reject his God. But try to point to any 'real world' that isn't, somewhere, being experienced.

attribution: George Berkeley · A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge
source_note: From the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710, public domain) — paraphrased.
